title: The 1927 Victor record date
summary: Wiggs names the players on his Victor date, including Diaz, Monk Hazel, Nappy Lamar and Charlie Hartman, and describes the long session.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Yeah, because your old Victor records had been made in the 20s. They were...
Yeah, they were under my right name, yeah.

When were they made about? Can you remember a little... Must have been 1926, huh? 1927, was it? We have the dope on it, I guess, probably on the record covers even. I think the Victor company kept records. Who all was on that? Can you remember anything about the date?
You mean the recording?
You don't mean the date of the year? No, I mean the recording section.
Yeah, I remember all about it.
You can tell us a little bit about that.

He was a piano player, a very good piano player, by the name of Diaz, who afterwards went to New York and played commercial music, and I guess he made a lot of money, and I don't blame him for playing commercial music. Hooray for him. He wasn't going to get stuck with this damn fool jazz business, you know, give your soul away and get nothing back. The hell with that. Diaz, who played a beautiful jazz piano, and Monk Hazel was on drums. Elry Mazin on clarinet, much to his disgust, since he was a saxophone player, and swore he couldn't play clarinet, but he played an awful nice clarinet on that record. But I don't think he's played clarinet since then, and he always swore that he could never play the instrument, but he did very well on that record. He was a good saxophone player. Who was the trombone player? Used to be the business manager of the union. What is his name? While we're thinking of him, Nappy Lamar was the guitar player, and that was the first record he ever made, you know, the Nappy Lamar with the Bob Crosby.
Now, let's see,
we've got to remember that trombone player.
You'll think of him in the middle. I can't think he does.
What is his name? Charlie Hartman.
Oh, sure.
Charlie Hartman. Later on was the business manager of the union. And myself on trumpet.
Actually, let me tell you this,

peculiar thing about making records in those days, sometimes they would only make one side, and sometimes they would make two sides. Well, I was lucky enough to have gotten in on the two-side date. But let me tell you, we started making those doggone things at nine o'clock in the morning, and stopped about two or three o'clock in the afternoon.
That long.
And they would take nothing but perfection. There was absolutely, they would take no, not the slightest hint of a flaw.
What building? Where were they made about?
They were made in the warehouse of wire lines. I think it was on Bienville Street, about the 500 block of Bienville Street. They had a warehouse.
